'''.onion''' is a special-use [[top-level domain]] name designating an anonymous [[Tor (network)#Onion services|onion service]], which was formerly known as a "hidden service",<ref>{{cite web |last1=Winter |first1=Philipp |title=How Do Tor Users Interact With Onion Services? |url=https://nymity.ch/onion-services/pdf/sec18-onion-services.pdf |access-date=27 December 2018}}</ref> reachable via the [[Tor (network)|Tor]] network. Such addresses are not actual [[Domain Name System|DNS names]], and the .onion TLD is not in the [[DNS root zone|Internet DNS root]], but with the appropriate proxy software installed, Internet programs such as [[web browser]]s can access sites with .onion [[URL|addresses]] by sending the request through the Tor network.

The "onion" name refers to [[onion routing]], the technique used by Tor to achieve a degree of [[anonymity]].

The purpose of using such a system is to make both the information provider and the person accessing the information more difficult to trace, whether by one another, by an intermediate network host, or by an outsider. Sites that offer dedicated .onion addresses may provide an additional layer of identity assurance via [[Extended Validation Certificate|EV HTTPS Certificates]] or [[Domain-validated certificate|Domain-validated HTTPS certificates]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tor Project {{!}} HTTPS for your Onion Service |url=https://community.torproject.org/onion-services/advanced/https/ |access-date=2026-02-22 |website=community.torproject.org}}</ref> Provision of an onion site also helps mitigate [[SSL stripping]] attacks by [[Tor (anonymity network)#Exit node eavesdropping|malicious exit nodes]] on the Tor network upon users who would otherwise access traditional HTTPS [[clearnet (networking)|clearnet]] sites over Tor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tor Project {{!}} How do Onion Services work? |url=https://community.torproject.org/onion-services/overview/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260204193505/https://community.torproject.org/onion-services/overview/ |archive-date=2026-02-04 |access-date=2026-02-22 |website=community.torproject.org |quote=Onion service traffic is encrypted from the client to the onion host. This is like getting strong SSL/HTTPS for free.}}</ref> Because connections to onion services do not use exit relays, they are not subject to exit node tampering.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tor Project {{!}} HTTPS for your Onion Service |url=https://community.torproject.org/onion-services/advanced/https/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260219135311/https://community.torproject.org/onion-services/advanced/https/ |archive-date=2026-02-19 |access-date=2026-02-22 |website=community.torproject.org |quote=When visiting a site over the Onion Services protocol, the Tor protocol prevents data in transit from being read or manipulated by man in the middle attacks, and the Onion Service protocol validates that the user is connected to the domain name in the browser address bar. No certificate authority is required for this proof, because the name of the service is the actual public key used to authenticate the underlying connection.}}</ref>

== Format ==
Addresses in the onion TLD are generally opaque, non-[[mnemonic]], alpha-numerical strings which are automatically generated based on a [[public key]] when an [[Tor (anonymity network)#Onion services|onion service]] is configured. These strings can be made up of any letter of the alphabet, and decimal digits from 2 to 7, representing in [[base32]] either an 80-bit [[Cryptographic hash function|hash]] ("version 2", or 16-character) or a 256-bit [[EdDSA#Ed25519|ed25519]] public key along with a version number and a checksum of the key and version number ("version 3", "next gen", or 56-character). As a result, in the past all combinations of sixteen base32 characters could potentially be valid version 2 addresses (though as the output of a cryptographic hash, a randomly selected string of this form having a corresponding onion service should be [[Preimage attack|extremely unlikely]]), while in the current version 3 only combinations of 56 base32 characters that correctly encoded an ed25519 public key, a checksum, and a version number (i.e., 3) are valid addresses.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://spec.torproject.org/rend-spec/encoding-onion-addresses.html|title=Encoding onion addresses [ONIONADDRESS] |website=spec.torproject.org|access-date=15 August 2026}}</ref>
It is possible to set up a partially human-readable .onion URL (e.g. starting with an organization name) by generating massive numbers of [[public-key cryptography|key pairs]] (a computational process that can be [[Parallel computing|parallelized]]) until a sufficiently desirable URL is found.<ref name="scallion">{{cite web | url=https://github.com/lachesis/scallion | title=Scallion | publisher=GitHub | access-date=2 November 2024}}</ref><ref name="facebook url">{{cite mailing list | url=http://archives.seul.org/tor/talk/Oct-2014/msg00433.html | title=Re: Facebook brute forcing hidden services | publisher=Simple End-User Linux | mailing-list=tor-talk | date=31 October 2014 | access-date=2 November 2014 | author=Muffett, Alec}}</ref>

Beginning in October 2021, stable releases of Tor software no longer support V2 (16 character) addresses.<ref>{{cite web |title=V2 Onion Services Deprecation |url=https://support.torproject.org/onionservices/v2-deprecation/ |website=Tor Project &#124; Support |access-date=7 July 2024}}</ref>

== WWW to .onion gateways ==
Proxies into the Tor network like [[Tor2web]] allow access to onion services from non-Tor browsers and for search engines that are not Tor-aware. By using a gateway, users give up their own anonymity and trust the gateway to deliver the correct content. Both the gateway and the onion service can [[browser fingerprint|fingerprint]] the browser, and access user IP address data. Some proxies use caching techniques that claim to provide better page-loading<ref>{{cite web|url=https://onion.cab/?a=why|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140521220306/https://onion.cab/?a=why|url-status=dead|archive-date=21 May 2014|title=Onion.cab: Advantages of this TOR2WEB-Proxy|access-date=21 May 2014}}</ref> than the official [[Tor (anonymity network)#Tor Browser|Tor Browser]].

== .exit (defunct pseudo-top-level domain) ==
'''.exit''' was a [[pseudo-top-level domain]] used by [[Tor (anonymity network)|Tor]] users to indicate on the fly to the Tor software the preferred [[exit node]] that should be used while connecting to a service such as a [[World Wide Web|web server]], without having to edit the configuration file for Tor (''torrc'').

The syntax used with this domain was ''hostname'' + ''.exitnode'' + ''.exit'', so that a user wanting to connect to <nowiki>http://www.torproject.org/</nowiki> through node ''tor26'' would have to enter the URL ''<nowiki>http://www.torproject.org.tor26.exit</nowiki>''.

Example uses for this would include accessing a site available only to addresses of a certain country or checking if a certain node is working.

Users could also type ''exitnode.exit'' alone to access the IP address of ''exitnode''.

The .exit notation was deprecated as of version 0.2.9.8.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://gitweb.torproject.org/tor.git/tree/ReleaseNotes |title=Tor Release Notes |access-date=4 October 2017}}</ref> It is disabled by default as of version 0.2.2.1-alpha due to potential application-level attacks,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://gitweb.torproject.org/torspec.git/tree/address-spec.txt |title=Special Hostnames in Tor |access-date=30 June 2012}}</ref> and with the release of 0.3-series Tor as "stable"<ref>{{cite web|title=Tor 0.3.2.9 is released: We have a new stable series!|url=https://blog.torproject.org/tor-0329-released-we-have-new-stable-series|publisher=The Tor Project|access-date=7 May 2018}}</ref> may now be considered defunct.

== Official designation ==
The domain was formerly a [[pseudo-top-level domain]] host suffix, similar in concept to such endings as [[.bitnet]] and [[.uucp]] used in earlier times.

On 9 September 2015 [[ICANN]], [[Internet Assigned Numbers Authority|IANA]] and the [[IETF]] designated .onion as a 'special use domain', giving the domain an official status following a proposal from [[Jacob Appelbaum]] of the Tor Project and [[Facebook]] security engineer [[Alec Muffett]].<ref name="lwn-iana">{{cite news |author=Willis |first=Nathan |date=10 September 2015 |title=Tor's .onion domain approved by IETF/IANA |url=https://lwn.net/Articles/657056/ |publisher=[[LWN.net]]}}</ref><ref name="official">{{cite news|last1=Franceschi-Bicchierai|first1=Lorenzo|title=Internet Regulators Just Legitimized The Dark Web|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/internet-regulators-just-legitimized-the-dark-web/|access-date=10 September 2015|date=10 September 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Special-Use Domain Names|url=https://www.iana.org/assignments/special-use-domain-names/special-use-domain-names.xhtml|access-date=10 September 2015}}</ref>

== HTTPS support ==

Prior to the adoption of [[CA/Browser Forum]] Ballot 144, an [[HTTPS]] certificate for a .onion name could only be acquired by treating .onion as an Internal Server Name.<ref name="ballot144">{{cite web|title=CA/Browser Forum Ballot 144 – Validation rules for .onion names|date=18 February 2015 |url=https://cabforum.org/2015/02/18/ballot-144-validation-rules-dot-onion-names/|access-date=13 September 2015}}</ref> Per the CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements, these certificates could be issued, but were required to expire before 1 November 2015.<ref>{{cite web|title=Baseline Requirements for the Issuance and Management Publicly-Trusted Certificates, v1.0|url=https://cabforum.org/wp-content/uploads/Baseline_Requirements_V1.pdf|access-date=13 September 2015|archive-date=14 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160114183223/https://www.cabforum.org/wp-content/uploads/Baseline_Requirements_V1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Despite these restrictions, [[DuckDuckGo]] launched an onion site with a self-signed certificate in July 2013;<ref>{{cite web|title=We've updated our Tor hidden service to work over SSL. No solution for the cert. warning, yet!|url=https://www.reddit.com/r/duckduckgo/comments/1hdqs6/weve_updated_our_tor_hidden_service_to_work_over/|website=[[Reddit]] r/duckduckgo|author=_zekiel|date=1 July 2013|access-date=20 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150428033600/https://www.reddit.com/r/duckduckgo/comments/1hdqs6/weve_updated_our_tor_hidden_service_to_work_over/|archive-date=28 April 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Facebook]] obtained the first SSL Onion certificate to be issued by a Certificate authority in October 2014,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Muffett|first1=Alec|title=Making Connections to Facebook more Secure|url=https://www.facebook.com/notes/protect-the-graph/making-connections-to-facebook-more-secure/1526085754298237|access-date=11 September 2015|date=31 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141031130553/https://www.facebook.com/notes/protect-the-graph/making-connections-to-facebook-more-secure/1526085754298237|archive-date=31 October 2014|url-status=dead|work=Protect the Graph|publisher=[[Facebook]]}}</ref> [[Blockchain.info]] in December 2014,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Alyson|title=Improved Security for Tor Users|url=https://blog.blockchain.com/2014/12/03/improved-security-for-tor-users/|access-date=11 September 2015|date=3 December 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141220203411/https://blog.blockchain.com/2014/12/03/improved-security-for-tor-users/|archive-date=20 December 2014|url-status=dead|work=[[Blockchain.info]] blog}}</ref> and [[The Intercept]] in April 2015.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Lee|first1=Micah|title=Our SecureDrop System for Leaks Now Uses HTTPS|url=https://theintercept.com/2015/04/08/securedrop-tor-hidden-service-now-uses-https/|access-date=10 September 2015|date=8 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151225060727/https://theintercept.com/2015/04/08/securedrop-tor-hidden-service-now-uses-https/|archive-date=25 December 2015|url-status=live|work=[[The Intercept]]}}</ref> ''[[The New York Times]]'' later joined in October 2017, but discontinued the site in April 2025.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://open.nytimes.com/https-open-nytimes-com-the-new-york-times-as-a-tor-onion-service-e0d0b67b7482 | title = The New York Times is Now Available as a Tor Onion Service | author-link = Runa Sandvik | last = Sandvik | first = Runa | date = 4 March 2025 | orig-date = 27 October 2017 | website = [[The New York Times|NYT]] Open blog | access-date = 26 April 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260426004507/https://open.nytimes.com/https-open-nytimes-com-the-new-york-times-as-a-tor-onion-service-e0d0b67b7482?gi=3fe55bdc6c90|archive-date=26 April 2026|url-status=live}}</ref>

Following the adoption of CA/Browser Forum Ballot 144 and the designation of the domain as 'special use' in September 2015, .onion meets the criteria for RFC 6761.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Arkko|first1=Jari|title=.onion|url=https://www.ietf.org/blog/2015/09/onion/|access-date=13 September 2015|date=10 September 2015}}</ref>  Certificate authorities may issue SSL certificates for HTTPS .onion sites per the process documented in the [[CA/Browser Forum]]'s Baseline Requirements,<ref>{{cite web|title=Baseline Requirements Documents|date=4 September 2013 |url=https://cabforum.org/baseline-requirements-documents/|access-date=13 September 2015}}</ref> introduced in Ballot 144.<ref name="ballot144"/>

As of August 2016, 13 onion domains are https signed across 7 different organisations via [[DigiCert]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Jamie Lewis|first1=Sarah|title=OnionScan Report: July 2016 – HTTPS Somewhere Sometimes|url=https://mascherari.press/onionscan-report-july-2016-https-somewhere-sometimes/|access-date=15 August 2016|date=7 August 2016}}</ref>
